A mechanism, then a system

I developed a twelve-joint quadruped with teammates, working across mechanical design, printed actuators, kinematics, electronics, and control software.

The design has changed as assembly and testing exposed problems that were easy to miss in CAD. My contribution includes the body and leg structures, actuator interfaces, analytical leg models, Python prototypes, and the later C++ control work. The project is still in development.

How the CAD evolved

  1. Early team design

    Package the robot around modular joints

    The early body and leg assemblies established the actuator interfaces and overall arrangement. These views are CAD concepts, rather than photographs of a finished robot.

  2. Assembly review

    Make the geometry practical to assemble

    The project review identified difficult countersunk-bolt access, bulky hip structures, tight fits, and missing provisions for batteries, electronics, and wiring. Those issues became specific revision questions.

  3. August–September 2026 captures

    Open the frame and revisit the joint structure

    Later CAD captures show an exposed frame layout and revised joint structures. I used component-level work to consider material removal, bearing seats, wiring access, and serviceability.

Dates identify the source captures. Team CAD is credited as collaborative work; a CAD view alone does not establish that the pictured revision was manufactured.

From CAD to a printed component

The important comparison is between the intended shape, the part that can actually be printed and assembled, and the behavior under load. Fit, access, print direction, and local stiffness each need a separate check.

The derivations behind the motion

I began with geometric forward and inverse kinematics, then revisited the Jacobian through component derivatives and homogeneous transforms. The handwritten revisions show the intermediate reasoning and corrections.

Integrate through smaller tests

I worked through motor signs, encoder references, gear ratios, CAN communication, and staged leg tests. Teammates contributed to assembly and subsystems such as IMU communication. Keeping those interfaces understandable made it easier to isolate a mechanical problem from a coordinate or communication problem.

What the project has demonstrated

WHAT THIS ESTABLISHES

Built hardware and coordinated motion; locomotion development continues.

The project has produced coordinated leg trajectories and limited locomotion. Reliable forward walking and robust terrain traversal remain development goals. The operating robot uses off-the-shelf motor drivers; the first custom motor-controller PCB did not reach working operation.
